extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of derivative-based theorems (Rolle, mean value, Darboux, inverse function, Taylor) and the start of Riemann integral theory; aimed at teaching precise hypotheses and consequences used in analysis. Contains definitions, propositions, proofs, examples and exercises for students learning rigorous calculus/real analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior extrema imply critical point
rubrics_metrics.description: If a differentiable function has a local minimum or maximum at an interior point of an interval then that interior point is a critical point (the derivative there is zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard calculus fact used to locate extrema: find critical points and endpoints and compare values. (Used as motivation for Rolle's theorem.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolle's theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f:[a,b] → ℝ be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) and suppose f(a)=f(b). Then there exists c in (a,b) such that f'(c)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric idea: if endpoints have same height, the function attains interior min or max so tangent horizontal. Hypotheses are essential: continuity on closed interval and differentiability on open interval (counterexamples if derivative fails to exist somewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of derivative existence on (a,b) in Rolle's theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: The derivative must exist for all x in (a,b) in the hypotheses of Rolle's theorem; otherwise the conclusion can fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes counterexamples where f is continuous on [a,b] but not differentiable at an interior point so no c with f'(c)=0 exists (illustrates necessity of differentiability hypothesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean Value Theorem (MVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f:[a,b] → ℝ be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b). Then there exists c in (a,b) such that f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: there is a tangent whose slope equals the secant slope between endpoints. Proof via Rolle's theorem by subtracting the affine line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)). Typical application: convert difference quotients into exact derivative values at some point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's mean value theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f and φ be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) with φ' not vanishing on (a,b). Then there exists c in (a,b) such that (f(b)-f(a))φ'(c) = (φ(b)-φ(a))f'(c) (equivalently f'(c)/φ'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(φ(b)-φ(a))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes the MVT. The proof follows by applying Rolle's theorem to a suitable combination of f and φ. Useful in proving L'Hôpital-type results and other ratio-based conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative zero on interval implies constant function (Proposition 4.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:I→ℝ is differentiable on interval I and f'(x)=0 for all x in I, then f is constant on I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via the mean value theorem: for any x<y pick c with f'(c)=(f(y)-f(x))/(y-x)=0 so f(y)=f(x). Typical use to show uniqueness up to constants when derivatives coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of monotonicity via derivative (Proposition 4.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let I be an interval and f:I→ℝ differentiable. (i) f is increasing iff f'(x) ≥ 0 for all x in I. (ii) f is decreasing iff f'(x) ≤ 0 for all x in I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One direction: if f increasing then difference quotients ≥0 and taking limit gives f'≥0. The other uses MVT to show f(y)-f(x)=f'(c)(y-x) and sign of f' determines monotonicity. Exercises address strict vs non-strict versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict monotonicity from strict sign of derivative (Proposition 4.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f':I→ℝ satisfies f'(x)>0 for all x in I then f is strictly increasing on I. If f'(x)<0 for all x then f is strictly decreasing. The converse need not hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Converse counterexample: function can be strictly increasing while derivative is zero at some points (e.g., x^3). Proof is via MVT. The proposition is used to guarantee injectivity and invertibility on intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: First derivative test for extrema (Proposition 4.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) and let c∈(a,b). (i) If f'(x) ≤ 0 for x in (a,c) and f'(x) ≥ 0 for x in (c,b) then f has an absolute minimum at c. (ii) If f'(x) ≥ 0 for x in (a,c) and f'(x) ≤ 0 for x in (c,b) then f has an absolute maximum at c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a sufficient condition for an absolute extremum from one-sided monotonicity deduced from derivative signs. The text notes converses do not necessarily hold and gives exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiability at endpoints via derivative limits (Proposition 4.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) If f:(a,b)→ℝ is differentiable on (a,b) and lim_{x→a+} f'(x)=L then f is differentiable at a with f'(a)=L; similarly at b. (ii) If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and lim_{x→a+} f'(x)=lim_{x→b-} f'(x)=L then the corresponding endpoint derivatives equal L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endpoint differentiability can be deduced from one-sided limits of the derivative. The text references an exercise and an extension result removing the need for f to be defined at the endpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darboux's theorem (intermediate value property for derivatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is differentiable on [a,b] and y lies strictly between f'(a) and f'(b), then there exists c in (a,b) such that f'(c)=y; i.e., f' has the intermediate value property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by subtracting a linear function of slope y and applying Rolle's theorem to the resulting function. Consequence: derivatives need not be continuous but cannot have jump discontinuities. Figure/motivation given in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of differentiable functions with discontinuous derivative (Example 4.2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist functions differentiable everywhere whose derivative is not continuous (example constructed shows derivative changes sign infinitely often near a point and is not continuous at that point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that Darboux property does not imply continuity; derivative can oscillate while still having intermediate value property. Shows necessity of additional hypotheses when assuming continuity of derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of C^1 (continuously differentiable)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:I→ℝ is differentiable and f' is continuous on I, then f is said to be continuously differentiable and written f∈C^1(I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common regularity class used throughout; when f' is continuous and nonzero one gets stronger conclusions (e.g., inverse function continuously differentiable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor polynomial (Definition 4.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n-times differentiable f near x0, the nth order Taylor polynomial at x0 is P^n_{x0}(x) = sum_{k=0}^n f^{(k)}(x0)/k! * (x-x0)^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This polynomial agrees with f and its derivatives at x0 up to order n. Figures illustrate approximations (e.g., sine). Used as the algebraic approximation in Taylor's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder (Theorem 4.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has n continuous derivatives on [a,b], then for distinct x0 and x in [a,b] there exists c between x0 and x such that f(x) = P^n_{x0}(x) + f^{(n+1)}(c)/(n+1)! * (x-x0)^{n+1}. (Lagrange form of remainder.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives precise error term: remainder evaluated at some intermediate c. Proof uses repeated application of MVT. Other remainder forms exist but Lagrange form is emphasized. c depends on x and x0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor series and analyticity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is infinitely differentiable, its Taylor series at x0 is sum_{k=0}^∞ f^{(k)}(x0)/k! (x-x0)^k. A function is analytic if its Taylor series at every point converges to f on some open interval containing that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: infinite differentiability does not guarantee convergence of the Taylor series to f; exercises and examples are provided where the Taylor series fails to represent the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second derivative test (Proposition 4.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is twice continuously differentiable on (a,b), f'(x0)=0 and f''(x0)>0, then f has a strict relative minimum at x0 (analogously f''(x0)<0 gives strict relative maximum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Taylor's theorem with n=1 and positivity of second derivative near x0. Continuity of f'' simplifies proof; stronger n-th derivative tests are left as exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma on derivative of inverse (Lemma 4.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let I,J be intervals and f:I→J differentiable at x0 with f'(x0)≠0 and f invertible onto J. Then the inverse g=f^{-1} is differentiable at y0=f(x0) and g'(y0)=1/f'(x0). If f' is continuous and never zero on I then f^{-1} is continuously differentiable on J.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation relates slopes of inverse/composition. Proof uses composition and continuity of an auxiliary quotient function. Important hypothesis: f'(x0)≠0 and local monotonicity/injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse function theorem (Theorem 4.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is continuously differentiable on (a,b) and f'(x0)≠0 at some x0∈(a,b), then there exists an open interval I containing x0 such that the restriction f|_I is injective onto an interval J and has a continuously differentiable inverse g:J→I with g'(y)=1/f'(g(y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local invertibility follows from nonvanishing derivative and continuity; monotonicity proposition is used to pick a suitable neighborhood. Gives explicit derivative formula for local inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: existence and differentiability of nth-root inverse
rubrics_metrics.description: For n∈ℕ and x>0 there exists a unique positive y with y^n = x; the inverse function g(x)=x^{1/n} is continuously differentiable on (0,∞) with derivative given by inverse-function formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of inverse function theorem to f(y)=y^n on (0,∞). Examples illustrate where inverse fails to be differentiable at 0 for certain n (vertical tangent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition and Darboux lower/upper sums (Definition 5.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A partition P of [a,b] is a finite set a=x0<x1<...<x_n=b. For bounded f on [a,b], on each subinterval [x_{i-1},x_i] define m_i = inf f, M_i = sup f. The lower Darboux sum L_{P,f} = sum_{i=1}^n m_i Δx_i and the upper Darboux sum U_{P,f} = sum_{i=1}^n M_i Δx_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: lower sums are areas of inscribed rectangles, upper sums of circumscribed rectangles. These sums are defined for any bounded function and are the building blocks of Darboux/Riemann integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds on Darboux sums (Proposition 5.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If m ≤ f(x) ≤ M for all x in [a,b] then for every partition P we have m(b-a) ≤ L_{P,f} ≤ U_{P,f} ≤ M(b-a). In particular the sets of lower and upper sums are bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes that sup of lower sums and inf of upper sums are finite and leads to definitions of the lower and upper Darboux integrals. Useful for proving integrability properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower and upper Darboux integrals (Definition 5.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower Darboux integral of f on [a,b] is sup_P L_{P,f} (supremum over all partitions P). The upper Darboux integral is inf_P U_{P,f}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riemann integrability is defined by equality of these two numbers (lower integral equals upper integral). The text notes common abuse of notation ∫_a^b f without mentioning variable of integration.
